fixes.explanation: Then the astrologers answered the king in Aramaic, "O king, may you live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will give the interpretation." Sounds polite, right? They're asking for the one thing they need to start. It's like a mechanic saying, "Just tell me what the noise sounds like," except the noise is inside the king's head.

The king doesn't say that. He tells them, "You have conspired to speak before me false and fraudulent words, hoping the situation will change." So he accuses them of conspiring to speak false words, not of being honest. He adds that if they tell him the dream, he will know they can give him its interpretation.

The king says, "You have conspired to speak before me false and fraudulent words, hoping the situation will change." Those are strong words. He accuses them of conspiring to speak false words, so he isn't saying they've been honest. He wants the dream told so he will know they can give him its interpretation.

Daniel asks, "Why is the decree from the king so harsh?" The text says that when Arioch, the commander of the king's guard, went out to execute the wise men, Daniel responded with discretion and tact. A question, not a speech. Then Arioch explained the situation to him.

Daniel never asks that. The text says he responds with discretion and tact, and what he asks is, "Why is the decree from the king so harsh?" He asks about the decree itself. Then Arioch explains the situation to him.
Daniel doesn't ask for soldiers. The text says men went to look for him and his friends! What he asks the king for is some time, so that he could give him the interpretation.

The text says that during the night, the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision, and he blessed the God of heaven. His response is praise, not a victory lap. Then he declares the praise out loud, and we get to hear it in the next verses.
With a decree like that hanging over him, I'd want a nap too. But the text doesn't have Daniel rolling over. It says the mystery was revealed to him in a vision, and he blessed the God of heaven.
That would be a smart move, but the text doesn't mention a scroll or a note. It says Daniel blessed the God of heaven and then declared his praise. That's the part the text gives us.

It's in his praise, word for word: "He changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them." Daniel declared this after he blessed the God of heaven (Daniel 2:19–20), with a king's decree hanging over him and his friends. I think he knows who is really in charge.

Daniel tells Arioch, "Do not execute the wise men of Babylon! Bring me before the king, and I will give him the interpretation." Arioch is the man the king appointed to destroy them, so this is a big ask. Daniel isn't only speaking up for himself here. He's speaking up for the whole group.
That's not what Daniel says. The astrologers told the king that no one on earth could do what he asked (Daniel 2:10). Daniel agrees that none of them can explain this mystery.
Daniel says the stone "…struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them." The stone was cut out, but not by human hands. The feet are where it lands.

Daniel says, "…the stone that had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth." A stone that ends up filling the whole earth. The statue got shattered and blown away, and the stone became a mountain.

Daniel says, "for iron shatters and crushes all things, and like iron that crushes all things, it will shatter and crush all the others." The picture is iron doing what iron does. This fourth kingdom does that to all the others.

Daniel says the kingdom God sets up "…will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people." So it doesn't change hands. He adds that it "…will shatter all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, but will itself stand forever."

Daniel says the God of heaven will set up a kingdom "…that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people." It's the one kingdom in this whole story that never gets passed along. It "…will itself stand forever." So this statement says the opposite of what Daniel says.

The text says King Nebuchadnezzar "…fell on his face, paid homage to Daniel…" This is the king who ordered the wise men destroyed. Now he's on the floor. I think that's a moment he did not see coming.

The king says, "Your God is truly the God of gods and Lord of kings, the Revealer of Mysteries, since you were able to reveal this mystery." A king says that about somebody else's God. Big words from a man who had become so angry and furious earlier in this chapter (Daniel 2:12).

The king made Daniel "…ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon." That's a long way from the decree that sent men to look for Daniel and his friends to execute them. Daniel ends the chapter with a big job.

It's right there in verse 48: the king "…made him ruler over the entire province of Babylon and chief administrator over all the wise men of Babylon." He got two jobs, and the second one is over the wise men. So the king does make him chief administrator over them.

At Daniel's request, the king appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to manage the province of Babylon. Those are the names given to Daniel's friends Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah (Daniel 1:6–7). They're the three he urged to plead for mercy from the God of heaven. Daniel remained in the king's court.
